\section{Methods: the validation test catalogue and its measured size and power}
\label{sec:validation-tests}

A bank that estimates its own default probabilities, loss rates and exposures, or that scores applicants with a statistical or a
machine-learning model, answers for the quality of those models to its supervisor and to its own management. The activity that
produces the answer is validation, and the risk it addresses is model risk: the potential for adverse consequences from decisions
based on incorrect or misused model outputs and reports \citep{validation-tests:sr117}. The United States supervisory guidance on
model risk management of April 2011 shaped the practice of most jurisdictions and was superseded on 17 April 2026 by the revised
guidance of the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
\citep{validation-tests:sr262}. In the euro area the European Central Bank expects every internal model to be validated initially and
at least annually, and lists the analyses that validation of a credit-risk model must contain: back-testing, discriminatory power,
representativeness, stability of the ratings and of the risk parameters, benchmarking and the quality of the input data; it asks the
institution to set quantitative thresholds for the back-testing, the discriminatory power and the stability analyses, and it asks that
the statistical tests be appropriate from a methodological point of view and sufficiently conservative \citep{validation-tests:ecb2025egim}.
The reporting instructions of February 2019 fix the statistics and the p-values of the back-testing of the probability of default
(a Jeffreys test per grade), of the comparison of the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve with its value at
development, of the stability of the migration matrix and of the concentration in rating grades, and fix no pass or fail threshold
\citep{credit-scoring:ecb2019}. The European Banking Authority guidelines on probability-of-default and loss-given-default
estimation require a review of the estimates with predefined metrics, thresholds and significance levels at least once a year
\citep{validation-tests:eba2018gl1716}, and the delegated regulation on the assessment methodology for the internal ratings-based approach
fixes the independence of the validation function, the annual back-testing of every rating system and the content of the validation
report \citep{validation-tests:eu2022rts439}. For machine-learning models the same supervisors add the validation of overfitting, of the
stability of the model against its hyperparameters and the randomness of its training, and of the explanation tools themselves
\citep{validation-tests:ecb2025egim,validation-tests:eba2023ml}.

The statistical instruments that these texts name are weaker than their regulatory use suggests. The Basel Committee working paper that
introduced most of them states that no really powerful tests of adequate calibration are available and that, because of the correlation
of defaults, there seems to be no way to develop such tests \citep{credit-scoring:bcbswp14}. A validator who applies a test with a
5 percent level needs three facts that the regulatory texts do not give: how often the test rejects a right model (its size), how often it
rejects a model with a defect of a known size (its power), and whether the statistic the test computes is the one its authors derived. The
fairness tests face the same question in another form. The four-fifths rule that is applied to selection rates in credit by analogy is an
employment benchmark, not a credit-law threshold \citep{validation-tests:cfr1607}, and the interagency fair-lending procedures state that
gross disparities in approval rates are not appropriate for an analysis of disproportionate adverse impact \citep{validation-tests:interagency2009}.
The section therefore treats a validation test as an instrument to be calibrated: it states each test with its theory, runs it against data
whose truth is known, and compares it with the published studies that measured it before.

Three cases of the product ask the questions of this section. Case C22, validating the validator, asks how often each validation test
rejects a right model and which defects it catches; its data are generators with planted defects, so that the true default probability, the
true correlation and the true shift are known and every rate carries its Monte Carlo error. Case C20, machine-learning model validation, asks
whether performance, drift, attribution and reason-code stability survive shocks the model has and has not seen, shifted populations, input
noise and retraining seeds, and whether the leakage screen catches a planted leak; it uses the Stressed German Credit Dataset, the Taiwan credit
card clients and the Polish companies bankruptcy files of the UCI repository, and the portfolios of the Federal Reserve supervisory scenarios as
shift probes. Case C21, fair-lending disparity testing, asks whether disparity tests find the same gaps in lending decisions from one year to the
next on the home-mortgage decisions of Delaware reported under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, in \vtCTwoOnePairs{} pairs of a fit year and a
confirmation year from \vtCTwoOneFirst{} to \vtCTwoOneLast{}.

The engine \vtfn{riskvalidation} \vtEngineVersion{} registers \vtCatTotal{} tests in \vtCatFamilies{} families, \vtCatPValue{} of which are decided by a
p-value (\cref{tab:vt-catalogue}). This section covers the \vtCatClassic{} tests of the calibration, discrimination, stability, rating-structure and
migration families (\cref{sec:m28}) and the \vtCatMl{} tests of the machine-learning and fairness families (\cref{sec:m29}); the tests of the other
families are the subject of the sections of their own methods. The third subsection (\cref{sec:m37}) states the measurement protocol and reruns the
three published studies that measured the size and power of these tests. The measured size and power of every test, the readings of the
three cases and the figures follow in \cref{sec:results-validation-tests}.

% method: the test catalogue of the calibration, discrimination, stability and rating families
\subsection{The test catalogue for probability-of-default calibration, discrimination, stability and rating structure}
\label{sec:m28}

Every test of the catalogue is a function that takes arrays or counts and returns one result object. The result carries the identifier of the
test, the statistic, the p-value or the metric, the null hypothesis, the alternative, the reference of the formula, the number of observations,
a hash of the inputs, the version of the policy that was applied, and a light. The light is the only place where a convention enters: a versioned
policy file holds, for each test, the kind of rule and two cut points, so that the light of a p-value test and of a metric test are
\begin{equation}
  \text{light}=\begin{cases}\text{red}&p<\alpha_{\mathrm{red}}\\ \text{amber}&p<\alpha_{\mathrm{amber}}\\ \text{green}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \text{light}=\begin{cases}\text{red}&m\ge m_{\mathrm{red}}\\ \text{amber}&m\ge m_{\mathrm{amber}}\\ \text{green}&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
  \label{eq:vt-light}
\end{equation}
where $p$ is the p-value, $m$ the metric, $\alpha_{\mathrm{amber}}=0.05$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{red}}=0.01$ in the default policy, and the cut points $m_{\mathrm{amber}}$
and $m_{\mathrm{red}}$ of a metric rule are those of the policy. Neither the ECB instructions nor the Basel working paper set a threshold, so the
5 and 1 percent levels are conventions that the policy names as such. A test that cannot be evaluated (one class missing, a variance of zero, a
statistic undefined) returns the light \emph{not evaluated} with its reason and no number; it is never coloured. \Cref{alg:vt-test} states the
evaluation of one test.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Evaluation of a registered validation test and its light.}
\label{alg:vt-test}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require test identifier $\tau$, inputs $x$, policy $\pi$
\State check the shape and the domain of every input; \textbf{raise} an error naming the field when an input is malformed
\If{the statistic is undefined for $x$ (no variance, one class, an empty group)}
  \State \Return a result with the light \emph{not evaluated}, the reason in the notes, and no statistic, metric or p-value
\EndIf
\State compute the statistic and its p-value $p$ (or the metric $m$) with the formula of the reference of $\tau$
\State read the rule and the cut points of $\tau$ in $\pi$; \textbf{if} $\pi$ holds no row for $\tau$ \textbf{return} \emph{not evaluated}
\State classify $p$ or $m$ with \cref{eq:vt-light}, strictly or inclusively as the row states
\State \Return the result with the reference, the null hypothesis, the alternative, the hash of $x$ and the version of $\pi$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Calibration of the probability of default.} Let a grade have $N$ obligors at the start of a year, $D$ defaults during it and a probability
of default $\mathrm{PD}$ applied. The Jeffreys test of the ECB gives the Beta$(1/2,1/2)$ prior to the true probability, so that its posterior is
Beta$(D+\tfrac12,N-D+\tfrac12)$ and the p-value is the posterior probability that the true probability is below the one applied,
\begin{equation}
  p_{\mathrm{J}}=F_{\mathrm{Beta}(D+\frac12,\,N-D+\frac12)}(\mathrm{PD}),
  \label{eq:vt-jeffreys}
\end{equation}
where $F$ in \cref{eq:vt-jeffreys} is the distribution function of the posterior; the null is that the applied probability is not below the true one, and the interval logic is
that of \citet{ratings:brown2001}. The binomial test has the p-value $P(\mathrm{Bin}(N,\mathrm{PD})\ge D)$ under independent defaults; the working paper
warns that its size can be much larger than its level when defaults are correlated. The correction of the working paper uses the one-factor model of
Vasicek: the asset value of an obligor is $\sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i+\sqrt{\rho}\,X$ with independent standard normal $X$ and $\varepsilon_i$ and
asset correlation $\rho$, an obligor defaults when its asset value is at most $\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{PD})$, and conditional on the systematic factor $X=x$ the
defaults are independent with probability $\mathrm{PD}(x)=\Phi\bigl((\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{PD})-\sqrt{\rho}\,x)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\bigr)$. The count is a binomial mixture,
\begin{equation}
  P(D\ge k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}P\bigl(\mathrm{Bin}(N,\mathrm{PD}(x))\ge k\bigr)\,\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad
  k^{*}=\min\{k:\;P(D\ge k)\le 1-q\},
  \label{eq:vt-mixture}
\end{equation}
where $\varphi$ is the standard normal density, $q$ the confidence level and the test rejects when $D\ge k^{*}$. The engine evaluates the integral with
Gauss-Hermite quadrature of 256 nodes. The definition of $k^{*}$ is the one that reproduces the critical counts that the working paper tabulates for a
probability of 1 percent, 1,000 obligors and $q=99$ percent, 19, 35, 49, 63 and 77 for asset correlations of 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 percent
\citep{credit-scoring:bcbswp14}; the 99 percent quantile of $D$ itself is one lower, and the engine adopts the definition that reproduces the print. Other parametric tests that incorporate dependence start from the Basel II model and use a granularity adjustment or moment matching \citep{validation-tests:tasche2003}.
Over several grades the chi-square test of the working paper sums the standardised differences,
\begin{equation}
  T=\sum_{i}\frac{(n_i p_i-d_i)^2}{n_i p_i(1-p_i)},
  \label{eq:vt-chi2}
\end{equation}
where, in \cref{eq:vt-chi2}, $n_i$, $d_i$ and $p_i$ are the obligors, the defaults and the probability applied in grade $i$; $T$ is asymptotically chi-square with as many degrees
of freedom as grades under independence. The test of the default profile ranks the calibrations of a probability-of-default curve by the shape and not
the level: given the total $D=\sum_i d_i$ the counts by grade are multinomial with the implied profile $q_i=n_ip_i/\sum_j n_jp_j$ and Pearson's statistic
$\sum_i(d_i-Dq_i)^2/(Dq_i)$ is referred to a Monte Carlo distribution, as \citet{ratings:tasche2013} does to rank calibrations of the S\&P default
curve. The Hosmer-Lemeshow statistic groups the obligors into $G$ groups of equal size by predicted probability, with observed defaults $O_g$, expected defaults
$E_g=\sum_{j\in g}p_j$ and size $m_g$,
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{HL}=\sum_{g=1}^{G}\frac{(O_g-E_g)^2}{E_g\,(1-E_g/m_g)},
  \label{eq:vt-hl}
\end{equation}
and \cref{eq:vt-hl} is referred to a chi-square law whose degrees of freedom are the object of a decision: the statistic was derived for a logistic model fitted on the same
data, with $G-2$ degrees of freedom \citep{credit-scoring:hosmer1980}, whereas a validator tests probabilities that were set before the outcomes on data the
model was not fitted to, for which each standardised group difference is asymptotically an independent chi-square variable with one degree of freedom and the
sum has $G$ \citep{credit-scoring:bcbswp14}. The engine uses $G$ by default and $G-2$ only for a model fitted on the sample, and the measured sizes of both
choices are in \cref{tab:vt-settings}. The test depends on the grouping \citep{validation-tests:hosmer1997} and its power grows with the sample size until small
departures are significant \citep{validation-tests:paul2013}. The Spiegelhalter test works on the forecasts $f_j$ and outcomes $d_j$ without binning:
\begin{align}
  E(\mathrm{BS})&=\frac1N\sum_j f_j(1-f_j), & \mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{BS})&=\frac1{N^2}\sum_j f_j(1-f_j)(1-2f_j)^2, & Z&=\frac{\mathrm{BS}-E(\mathrm{BS})}{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{BS})}},
  \label{eq:vt-spiegelhalter}
\end{align}
with $\mathrm{BS}$ the observed Brier score in \cref{eq:vt-spiegelhalter} and the p-value the upper normal tail \citep{credit-scoring:spiegelhalter1986,credit-scoring:brier1950}. The Brier score also decomposes exactly, for forecasts constant within each group, into reliability, resolution and uncertainty \citep{credit-scoring:murphy1973}, and the expected calibration error averages the absolute gap between the observed and the predicted default rate over $M$ quantile bins \citep{credit-scoring:naeini2015,validation-tests:guo2017}; both are descriptive and carry no light. Two tests use
several years: for forecasts $\mathrm{PD}_t$ and observed default rates $d_t$ over $T$ years the normal test is
\begin{equation}
  \hat\sigma^2=\frac1{T-1}\Bigl(\sum_t(d_t-\mathrm{PD}_t)^2-\frac1T\Bigl(\sum_t(d_t-\mathrm{PD}_t)\Bigr)^2\Bigr),\qquad Z=\frac{\sum_t(d_t-\mathrm{PD}_t)}{\sqrt T\,\hat\sigma},
  \label{eq:vt-normal}
\end{equation}
and \cref{eq:vt-normal} assumes independence over time; the traffic-lights test colours the standardised default rate of each year, $R_t=(D_t-N_tp_t)/\sqrt{N_tp_t(1-p_t)}$, green, yellow, orange or red at the cut-offs
$\Phi^{-1}(q_g)$, $\Phi^{-1}(q_g+q_y)$ and $\Phi^{-1}(q_g+q_y+q_o)$ with the probabilities $(q_g,q_y,q_o,q_r)=(0.5,0.3,0.15,0.05)$ of the working paper. Under the null the
colour counts $(A_g,A_y,A_o,A_r)$ over $T$ years are multinomial; the profiles are ordered by
\begin{equation}
  V=1000A_g+100A_y+10A_o+A_r,
  \label{eq:vt-traffic}
\end{equation}
and, with $V$ of \cref{eq:vt-traffic}, the p-value is $P[V\le V_{\mathrm{obs}}]$, computed by exact multinomial enumeration. A year whose standardised rate sits on a boundary needs a colour: the printed rule
gives the better colour and the simulation of the working paper must have given the worse one, a difference that the rerun of \cref{sec:m37} identified and that changes the
size by a factor of about four when a grade expects few defaults.

\paragraph{Discriminatory power.} With $A$ the defaulters and $B$ the non-defaulters the area under the curve is the Mann-Whitney statistic
$\mathrm{AUC}=|A|^{-1}|B|^{-1}\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{b\in B}u_{a,b}$, with $u_{a,b}$ equal to 1, $\tfrac12$ or 0 as the risk of $a$ is above, equal to or below that of $b$, the probability that a
defaulter is ranked riskier than a non-defaulter \citep{credit-scoring:hanley1982}. Its Gini form $2\,\mathrm{AUC}-1$ is the accuracy ratio of the cumulative accuracy profile and equals Somers'
$D$ \citep{validation-tests:somers1962}. The structural components $V_{10}(a)=|B|^{-1}\sum_bu_{a,b}$ and $V_{01}(b)=|A|^{-1}\sum_au_{a,b}$ give the variance used by the ECB and, with it,
the test against the area at development; the extension that the engine adds passes the variance of an estimated development area:
\begin{equation}
  s^2=\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(V_{10})}{|A|}+\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{var}}(V_{01})}{|B|},\qquad
  S=\frac{\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{init}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{curr}}}{s},\qquad
  S_{\mathrm{ext}}=\frac{\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{init}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{curr}}}{\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{curr}}^2+s_{\mathrm{init}}^2}},
  \label{eq:vt-auc}
\end{equation}
with the p-value $1-\Phi(S)$ and the null that the area at development is smaller than the current one. The statistic $S$ of \cref{eq:vt-auc} treats the development area as a constant; when it was estimated
on a sample of the same size the difference has twice the variance the test assumes, which $S_{\mathrm{ext}}$ corrects. To compare a champion and a challenger scored on the same obligors the
engine implements the nonparametric test of \citet{credit-scoring:delong1988}, $z=(\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}_1-\widehat{\mathrm{AUC}}_2)/\sqrt{\mathbf S_{11}+\mathbf S_{22}-2\mathbf S_{12}}$ with $\mathbf S=S_{10}/|A|+S_{01}/|B|$
the covariance matrix of the placements of the two models. The test is valid for models of different families validated on a holdout; for nested models fitted on the sample on which they are compared, its null
distribution is not normal when the added predictor is unrelated to the outcome \citep{validation-tests:demler2012}.

\paragraph{Stability and rating structure.} The population stability index of $B$ fixed bins with development proportions $e_i$ and current proportions $a_i$ is
$\mathrm{PSI}=\sum_i(a_i-e_i)\ln(a_i/e_i)$, the symmetrised Kullback-Leibler divergence. The rule of thumb that reads it below 0.10 as little change and above 0.25 as significant change has no
reference to type I or type II error \citep{credit-scoring:yurdakul2020}; the same authors show that, for samples of $n$ and $m$ observations, $(1/n+1/m)^{-1}\mathrm{PSI}$ is approximately chi-square with
$B-1$ degrees of freedom, so that
\begin{equation}
  \text{reject}\iff \mathrm{PSI}>\Bigl(\frac1n+\frac1m\Bigr)\chi^2_{1-\alpha,\,B-1},
  \label{eq:vt-psi}
\end{equation}
and the engine applies \cref{eq:vt-psi} and reports the light of this benchmark with the conventional bands as a note. The benchmark reproduces the values 0.338, 0.169, 0.085 and 0.034 that their Table 2 gives for ten bins, $\alpha=5$ percent and $n=m$ equal to 100, 200, 400 and
1,000. The characteristic stability index is the same formula on the bins of one model input; the chi-square test of homogeneity of the $2\times B$ table and the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test complete the family, and the
Wasserstein-1 distance is reported without a threshold. For the rating system, the migration z-tests of the ECB compare each off-diagonal frequency with its neighbour closer to the diagonal,
$z_{ij}=(p_{i,j+1}-p_{ij})/\sqrt{p_{ij}(1-p_{ij})/N_i+p_{i,j+1}(1-p_{i,j+1})/N_i+2p_{ij}p_{i,j+1}/N_i}$ below the diagonal, and the engine adds a Holm step-down adjustment, labelled as its own, because the ECB specifies no
control over the many cells. The concentration test of the ECB refers the coefficient of variation of the grade frequencies to a normal law,
\begin{equation}
  CV=\sqrt{K\sum_{i=1}^{K}\Bigl(R_i-\frac1K\Bigr)^2},\qquad S(c)=\frac{\sqrt{K-1}\,(c-CV_{\mathrm{init}})}{c\sqrt{0.5+c^2}},
  \label{eq:vt-hhi}
\end{equation}
with $R_i$ the relative frequency of grade $i$, $K$ the number of grades and $c$ the current coefficient of variation. The function $S(c)$ of \cref{eq:vt-hhi} rises, peaks and falls back towards zero because the
denominator grows as $c^2$, so that its largest value over every possible current distribution can stay below the 5 percent critical value 1.645: with ten grades and an initial coefficient of
0.6 the largest value is 1.094. A test of this form cannot reject however concentrated the grades become, a property that is read in \cref{tab:vt-structure}.

\paragraph{Assumptions, parameters and complexity.} The tests assume what their authors derived: independent defaults within a year for the count tests, independence over time for the normal and
traffic-lights tests, bins fixed before the current sample is seen for the stability index, independent obligors within a row for the migration tests. The parameters of Contraste are conventions or choices made by
measurement. The levels are 5 and 1 percent; the Hosmer-Lemeshow grouping is $G=10$; the default-profile test uses 2,000 Monte Carlo draws; the bins of the stability tests are the ten deciles of the development
sample, with open outer edges so that every current value falls in a bin and an empty bin floored at half an observation of its own sample; the intervals of the discrimination statistics resample defaulters and
non-defaulters separately. The Jeffreys, binomial and Hosmer-Lemeshow cut points are those of the default policy and cite the ECB and the working paper as setting no thresholds. Complexity is low: the count tests
evaluate one regularised incomplete beta function or $Q=256$ of them, $O(Q)$, and the critical count of \cref{eq:vt-mixture} by bisection takes $O(Q\log N)$; the area under the curve and its variance are computed from
sorted placements in $O(n\log n)$; the Hosmer-Lemeshow statistic sorts by predicted probability in $O(n\log n)$; the stability indices count into bins in $O(n+B)$; the migration tests are $O(K^2)$ cells and the exact
traffic-lights distribution convolves $T$ years over the $\binom{T+3}{3}$ colour profiles.

\begingroup\emergencystretch=3em
\paragraph{Implementation and acceptance criterion.} The tests are the functions of the modules \vtfn{riskvalidation.validation.calibration}, \vtfn{discrimination}, \vtfn{stability}, \vtfn{rating_system} and
\vtfn{transitions} of \vtfn{riskvalidation} \vtEngineVersion{}, registered in \vtfn{riskvalidation.core.registry} and returned as \vtfn{TestResult} objects of \vtfn{riskvalidation.core.result}; the policy
is \vtfn{riskvalidation.core.policy.Policy} read from the packaged \vtfn{default.json}. The pipeline module \vtfn{data-pipeline/pipeline/cases/c22_validator.py} feeds them from the generators of
\vtfn{riskvalidation.generators}. Each test is compared against a published worked example or an independent reference, and the acceptance criterion is that it reproduces it to a stated tolerance and that every result
carries its reference, its null hypothesis and the version of the policy: the critical counts of the working paper, the benchmark values of \citet{credit-scoring:yurdakul2020}, the closed forms of the
distributions of SciPy, the placements of the ECB formulas, and the published simulations that \cref{sec:m37} reruns. The calibration of the Hosmer-Lemeshow degrees of freedom, of the traffic-lights tie rule and of the
extended AUC variance are findings of this comparison and not conventions inherited from a source.
\par\endgroup

% method: the machine-learning and fairness tests
\subsection{Validation tests for machine-learning models and for fairness}
\label{sec:m29}

The validation of a machine-learning credit model has the questions of the ECB guide for models with a complex structure: whether the complexity is justified against a simpler benchmark, whether the model is stable
with respect to the hyperparameters and the randomness of its training, whether it overfits, whether it performs out of sample and out of time, and whether its explanations are themselves stable and correct
\citep{validation-tests:ecb2025egim}. The follow-up report of the European Banking Authority on machine learning for internal ratings adds the analysis of the relationship of each risk driver with the output, the
detection of overfitting and the stability of the grade assignment \citep{validation-tests:eba2023ml}. The engine turns each question into a test with a statistic, a reference and a light; \cref{tab:vt-policy} lists the
rows of the policy that colour them, and every cut point is a convention proposed by the engine and labelled so, never a regulatory threshold.

\input{tables/validation-tests-policy}

\paragraph{Robustness, shift and generalisation.} Robustness to input noise perturbs the evaluation features only, never the training slice,
\begin{equation}
  \begin{gathered}
  \tilde x_{ij}=x_{ij}+\epsilon\,s_j\,z_{ij},\quad z_{ij}\sim N(0,1),\\
  \Delta_{\mathrm{AUC}}(\epsilon)=\mathrm{AUC}(\epsilon)-\mathrm{AUC}(0),\qquad\text{finding}\iff-\Delta_{\mathrm{AUC}}(\epsilon^{*})>\tau\end{gathered}
  \label{eq:vt-robust}
\end{equation}
where, in \cref{eq:vt-robust}, $s_j$ is the standard deviation of feature $j$, $\epsilon$ the noise scale, $\epsilon^{*}$ the preset scale and $\tau$ the tolerance in AUC points; the same standard normal draws are used at every scale, so that the
perturbed samples of a grid are nested. Resilience to a shift scores each evaluation row by the probability that a resemblance classifier assigns to the evaluation sample. The classifier is a ridge-penalised logistic
regression fitted by Newton's method on standardised features, with balanced class weights $w_i$, an unpenalised intercept and cross-fitting over five folds in which rows with an identical feature vector are never split,
\begin{equation}
  \hat\beta=\arg\min_\beta\sum_i w_i\bigl[\log(1+e^{z_i})-y_iz_i\bigr]+\frac{\lambda}{2}\lVert\beta_{1:p}\rVert^2,\qquad z_i=\beta_0+\beta_{1:p}^{\top}x_i,\quad\lambda=1.
  \label{eq:vt-shift-score}
\end{equation}
The model is then judged on the evaluation rows of highest shift score. These rows form a region of the feature space on which the AUC is lower by range restriction even without any shift, so that the raw drop of the AUC
is positive under the null; a first design that read it against fixed cut points had a size of 10.55 percent, and a second design that permuted the domain labels of the pooled rows put the shifted rows into its own null
and had a power of 28 percent. The light now reads the observed drop against the drops of random development subsets of the evaluation size (\cref{alg:vt-shift}),
\begin{equation}
  p=\frac{1+\#\{r:\ \Delta^{*}_r\ge\Delta_{\mathrm{obs}}\}}{R+1},
  \label{eq:vt-shift-p}
\end{equation}
which is valid under the null because the evaluation rows are then exchangeable with the development rows \citep{validation-tests:phipson2010}. The overfit gap is $M_{\mathrm{train}}-M_{\mathrm{test}}$ for a metric where higher is
better, flagged when it exceeds $\tau$, and the weak spots are the slices of at least 30 rows whose mean error exceeds a multiple $k$ of the overall mean.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{The development-only reference of the shift-resilience test.}
\label{alg:vt-shift}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require development features and labels $(X_d,y_d)$, evaluation features $X_e$ with $n_e$ rows, a fitted predictor, the share $h$ of worst rows, the number of draws $R$
\State require $|X_d|\ge 2n_e$ and the development labels; otherwise \Return \emph{not evaluated} with the reason
\State score each evaluation row by the cross-fitted resemblance probability of \cref{eq:vt-shift-score}; keep the $m=\lceil h\,n_e\rceil$ rows of highest score
\State $\Delta_{\mathrm{obs}}\gets\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{full}}-\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{worst}}$ on the evaluation rows
\For{$r=1,\dots,R$}
  \State draw without replacement $n_e$ development rows as a pseudo-evaluation set; the other development rows are the pseudo-development set
  \State refit the resemblance score, keep the $m$ worst pseudo-evaluation rows, and compute $\Delta^{*}_r$ as in line 3; skip the draw if that subsample holds a single class
\EndFor
\State \Return $p$ of \cref{eq:vt-shift-p}, with the observed drop as the statistic and the mean and 95th percentile of the null drops in the notes
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Seeds, explanations and the split-conformal coverage.} The stability across seeds is the sample standard deviation $s_A$ of the AUC of $K$ refits, $s_A=\sqrt{(K-1)^{-1}\sum_k(A_k-\bar A)^2}$, read beside the
share of obligors whose grade changes between seeds and the Kendall rank correlation of the attributions of two seeds. The reasons of an obligor in a refit are its four features of largest signed contribution towards the
event on the log-odds scale, and the stability of the reason codes is the mean share of the reasons kept between the first refit and each later one. The agreement of two explainers is the Spearman correlation $\rho$ between the
mean absolute SHAP value of each feature \citep{credit-scoring:lundberg2017,credit-scoring:lundberg2020} and the range of its accumulated local effect curve \citep{validation-tests:apley2020}, and the additivity of the attributions is checked
by
\begin{equation}
  f(x)=\phi_0+\sum_i\phi_i,\qquad \text{gap}=\max_r\Bigl|f(x_r)-\bigl(\phi_0+\sum_i\phi_{ri}\bigr)\Bigr|,
  \label{eq:vt-additivity}
\end{equation}
with $\phi_i$ the Shapley value of feature $i$ in \cref{eq:vt-additivity}. The partial dependence and individual conditional expectation curves complete the effect checks \citep{validation-tests:friedman2001,validation-tests:goldstein2015}. The conformal coverage test
takes the scores $s_i$ of $n_{\mathrm{cal}}$ calibration points, the rank $k=\lceil(n_{\mathrm{cal}}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ computed in exact decimal arithmetic, the quantile $\hat q$ equal to the $k$-th smallest score, and the set
$C(x)=\{y:s(x,y)\le\hat q\}$, whose coverage is at least $1-\alpha$ under exchangeability \citep{validation-tests:angelopoulos2021,validation-tests:vovk2022}. Over draws of the calibration set, the coverage conditional on it is Beta$(k,n_{\mathrm{cal}}+1-k)$ distributed, so that the number of covered
points among $m$ test rows is Beta-Binomial,
\begin{equation}
  c\sim\mathrm{BetaBin}(m,\,k,\,n_{\mathrm{cal}}+1-k),\qquad p=\sum_{c':\,P(c')\le P(c_{\mathrm{obs}})}P(c'),
  \label{eq:vt-conformal}
\end{equation}
and the light reads the p-value of \cref{eq:vt-conformal}. The plain binomial p-value ignores the randomness of the calibration quantile and over-rejects: it has a size of 6.2, 16.25 and 38.0 percent when the test window is a tenth, equal to and four times the
calibration window, whereas the Beta-Binomial p-value has sizes of 4.75, 4.93 and 5.22 percent at the same ratios (engine documentation, 4,000 repetitions). The leakage screen reads four signals: a feature value dated after the observation date, a single feature of
$\max(\mathrm{AUC}_j,1-\mathrm{AUC}_j)$ above 0.95, a test entity present in training, and a cross-fitted resemblance AUC of development against out-of-time above 0.70. Data quality counts the failed cells or rows of six checks
(completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness and label consistency). The estimate of the AUC without labels follows the expected confusion counts of a calibrated probability $\hat p_j$,
$TP=\sum_{\hat y_j=1}\hat p_j$ and $FP=\sum_{\hat y_j=1}(1-\hat p_j)$, and is always an estimate with four stated assumptions, never a light; the comparison of a champion and a challenger is the paired bootstrap interval of the
Brier difference $d_i=(q_i-y_i)^2-(p_i-y_i)^2$.

\paragraph{Fairness.} For a protected attribute $A$, a decision $\hat Y$ and an outcome $Y$, demographic parity is the equality of the selection rates $r_g=x_g/n_g$ of the groups, measured by the difference $\Delta_g=r_g-r_{\mathrm{ref}}$ and the
ratio $\rho_g=r_g/r_{\mathrm{ref}}$; equalized odds and equal opportunity equalise the true and false positive rates $P(\hat Y=1\mid A=g,Y=y)$ \citep{validation-tests:hardt2016}; the calibration within groups and the area under the curve by group are the engine's
own tests applied inside each group \citep{validation-tests:kozodoi2022,credit-scoring:naeini2015}. The four-fifths indicator is decided on the integer counts, against the group of highest rate $h$,
\begin{equation}
  \text{flag}_g\iff 5\,x_g\,n_h<4\,x_h\,n_g,
  \label{eq:vt-fourfifths}
\end{equation}
so that \cref{eq:vt-fourfifths} never forms the ratio of floating-point rates, which misjudges a pair that is exactly four-fifths ($0.6/0.75$ is $0.7999\ldots$ in floating point). It is labelled an employment benchmark \citep{validation-tests:cfr1607}. For two groups the pooled two-proportion test and the sample odds ratio of Fisher's exact test are, as \cref{eq:vt-ztest} states,
\begin{equation}
  \hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2},\qquad z=\frac{x_1/n_1-x_2/n_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}},\qquad \widehat{\mathrm{OR}}=\frac{x_1(n_2-x_2)}{(n_1-x_1)\,x_2}.
  \label{eq:vt-ztest}
\end{equation}
The controlled disparity fits a logistic decision model on the protected indicators $a_{ij}$ and the permitted controls $c_{il}$,
$\mathrm{logit}\,P(\hat Y_i=1)=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_ja_{ij}+\sum_l\gamma_lc_{il}$, by iteratively reweighted least squares, $\beta^{(t+1)}=\beta^{(t)}+(X^{\top}WX)^{-1}X^{\top}(y-\mu)$ with $W=\mathrm{diag}(\mu_i(1-\mu_i))$, and reports the odds ratio $e^{\hat\beta}$ with a
Wald interval; a linear model does the same for the rate spread. Replication refits the estimate on the next year and compares its sign and size. Situation testing follows the counterfactual algorithm of
\citet{validation-tests:alvarez2025}: for each complainant $c$ of the protected group the distance to every row is the mean of the overlap measure for categorical attributes and the range-normalised absolute difference for continuous ones,
the $k$ nearest rows of the protected group and of the other groups give the shares of negative decisions $p_c$ and $p_t$, and the claim is significant when
\begin{equation}
  \Delta p=p_c-p_t,\qquad w_\alpha=z_\alpha\sqrt{\frac{p_c(1-p_c)+p_t(1-p_t)}{k}},\qquad \Delta p-w_\alpha>\tau,
  \label{eq:vt-situation}
\end{equation}
with $z_\alpha=\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$ and $\tau$ the accepted deviation in \cref{eq:vt-situation}. Public mortgage data carry no loan outcome, so the four outcome-conditioned tests never run on case C21, and the ceteris paribus comparator is the only one run because the data give
no counterfactual dataset.

\paragraph{Assumptions, parameters and complexity.} The tests of a robustness curve describe how a predictor reacts to noise proportional to the column spread and not whether the inputs carry that noise; the shift score ranks rows by distance from the development sample and does not say the
shift matters; a stable AUC across seeds is not a stable model; the conformal coverage is marginal and not conditional on a segment; a fairness disparity describes a sample and not its cause. The parameters in Contraste are the cut points of \cref{tab:vt-policy}, the noise grid of case C20 (0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 and 1 times the feature
spread, with the preset scale 0.1), 20 retraining seeds and 100 refits for the reason codes, the top four reasons as the reason codes, a worst share of 0.1 and 199 development draws for the shift reference, the 90 percent conformal level, $k=30$ and $\alpha=0.05$ for the situation test with the range normalisation, and the 95 percent level of the
intervals. They were chosen by measurement where a planted defect allowed it: the amber cut of the situation-testing share is 0.20 because at 0.10 the rule raised a false alarm on about one null draw in five, the complainants sharing neighbours so that the significant share is more variable than a binomial count. Complexity follows the
algorithms: a robustness grid costs one prediction pass per scale, $O(|\text{grid}|\,np)$; the shift reference refits the resemblance score $R+1$ times with five folds each, each fit a Newton iteration of $O(np^2+p^3)$ per step; the conformal quantile sorts in $O(n\log n)$; the logistic decision model costs $O(q^2n+q^3)$ per Newton step for $q$
coefficients; the situation test computes the distance of each complainant to every row, $O(c\,np)$ for $c$ complainants, and selects the $k$ nearest.

\begingroup\emergencystretch=3em
\paragraph{Implementation and acceptance criterion.} The tests are the functions of \vtfn{riskvalidation.validation.ml} and \vtfn{riskvalidation.validation.fairness} of \vtfn{riskvalidation} \vtEngineVersion{}, over the modules \vtfn{riskvalidation.ml} (\vtfn{robustness}, \vtfn{seeds}, \vtfn{explanations},
\vtfn{effects}, \vtfn{generalisation}, \vtfn{conformal}, \vtfn{leakage}, \vtfn{dataquality}, \vtfn{cbpe}, \vtfn{challenger}) and \vtfn{riskvalidation.fairness} (\vtfn{metrics}, \vtfn{inference}, \vtfn{conditional}, \vtfn{replication}, \vtfn{situation}). The engine imports no learning library: the model is a predict callable and
the attributions are arrays computed by the pipeline modules \vtfn{data-pipeline/pipeline/cases/c20} and \vtfn{c21} with the pinned explanation library. The acceptance criterion is that each test detects its planted defect on the generator with its power reported at the 5 percent level and holds its size under the null within Monte Carlo error. The planted-defect generators are frozen configurations with an exact truth and a
verifier (a leak column whose single-feature AUC is $\Phi(s/\sqrt2)$ exactly, a covariate shift, a noise-sensitive signal whose AUC at scale $\epsilon$ is known in closed form, a seed-unstable model, an exchangeability break, a threshold bias, a label-noise bias and a proxy feature). The engine's design bound is a size of at most 0.05 plus two Monte Carlo standard errors and a power of
at least 0.90; the reconciliations against independent implementations are those of fairlearn for the equalized-odds difference, of statsmodels for the two-proportion test and the logistic and linear decision models, and of MAPIE for the conformal quantile.
\par\endgroup

% method: the rerun of the published size and power studies
\subsection{Rerun of the published size and power studies of the validation tests}
\label{sec:m37}

Three studies measured the size and power of the tests of \cref{sec:m28}: the simulation of the Basel Committee working paper for the normal and traffic-lights tests \citep{credit-scoring:bcbswp14}, the simulation of \citet{credit-scoring:yurdakul2020}
for the population stability index and its chi-square benchmark, and the simulation of \citet{validation-tests:demler2012} for the DeLong test on nested models. The product reruns all three, cell by cell, with the generator, the tests and the harness of the engine.
The design follows the structure of \citet{alm:morris2019}: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures. The estimand is the true rejection probability of a test at a level; the performance measure is the rejection rate with its Monte Carlo
standard error. With $n$ repetitions and $k$ rejections the rate $\hat r=k/n$ has
\begin{equation}
  \widehat{\mathrm{SE}}(\hat r)=\sqrt{\frac{\hat r(1-\hat r)}{n}},\qquad
  \Bigl[\frac{\hat r+\frac{z^2}{2n}\pm z\sqrt{\frac{\hat r(1-\hat r)}{n}+\frac{z^2}{4n^2}}}{1+\frac{z^2}{n}}\Bigr],
  \label{eq:vt-mcse}
\end{equation}
the second expression being the Wilson interval, which stays inside $[0,1]$ and behaves near zero where small sizes sit, and is recommended for a binomial proportion \citep{ratings:brown2001}. The review of \citet{alm:morris2019} found that 93 of 100 simulation studies in one volume of Statistics in Medicine did not report
the Monte Carlo error; every rate of the engine carries it. Under the null at its boundary the true rejection rate is at most $\alpha$, so a measured size is judged one-sided: a test holds its size when
\begin{equation}
  \hat r\le\alpha+z_{0.999}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha(1-\alpha)}{n}},
  \label{eq:vt-sizebound}
\end{equation}
which is \vtBoundFive{} percent at $\alpha=5$ percent and \vtBoundOne{} percent at $\alpha=1$ percent for the repetitions of \cref{tab:vt-size}. A rate above it is not Monte Carlo noise at the 0.1 percent level. Against an exact probability $\pi$ the comparison is two-sided, $|\hat r-\pi|\le 3.29\sqrt{\pi(1-\pi)/n}$. Against
a published rate $r'$ of $n'$ runs both numbers are estimates of one true rate, so the difference is judged by its standard error at the pooled rate,
\begin{equation}
  \bar r=\frac{k+r'n'}{n+n'},\qquad z=\frac{\hat r-r'}{\sqrt{\bar r(1-\bar r)\,(1/n+1/n')}},\qquad\text{agree}\iff|z|\le 3.29,
  \label{eq:vt-agree}
\end{equation}
and 3.29 is the two-sided 0.1 percent point of the normal law. The streams of the repetitions are independent: one stream per repetition is spawned from one seed, so that repetition $i$ reruns alone to the same data and a test that carries its own randomness receives a seed drawn from the repetition's stream after the data, never a constant.
The comparison is the acceptance criterion of the product for this method: each published cell agrees with the rerun within the bound of \cref{eq:vt-agree} or the disagreement is stated. The number of agreeing cells is a result of the rerun, reported in \cref{sec:results-validation-tests}, and not a threshold fixed beforehand.

The generator of the working-paper study is the extension in the time dimension of the Vasicek model. A fixed portfolio is observed over years $t=1,\dots,T$ with $N_t$ obligors, the change in the economic conditions is the standard normal factor $S_t$ with $\mathrm{corr}(S_s,S_t)=\vartheta^{|s-t|}$, and
conditional on the factors the defaults are binomial with
\begin{equation}
  p_t(S)=\Phi\Bigl(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p_t)-\sqrt{\rho_t}\,S_t}{\sqrt{1-\rho_t}}\Bigr).
  \label{eq:vt-wp14-generator}
\end{equation}
The study of the working paper, run with the generator of \cref{eq:vt-wp14-generator}, uses five years of 1,000 obligors in eight scenarios for the type I error (independence or a factor correlation of 0.2, asset correlations 0.05 to 0.09, small or large and constant or varying probabilities) and four for the type II error (true probabilities 0.05 or 0.5 percentage points above the forecasts), each with 25,000 runs. The engine's generator
reproduces the correlation of two defaults that the working paper tabulates: with the bivariate normal distribution $\Phi_2$ the joint default probability of two obligors is $\pi_2=\Phi_2(c,c;\rho)$ with $c=\Phi^{-1}(p)$, the variance of a year's count is $Np(1-p)+N(N-1)(\pi_2-p^2)$ and the default correlation is $(\pi_2-p^2)/(p(1-p))$. The study of Yurdakul and Naranjo draws $n$ observations from
$N(0,64)$, a second sample of $m$ observations from $N(\mu_2,64)$ with $\mu_2$ equal to 0, 2 or 4 (shifts of 0, 1/4 and 1/2 standard deviations), bins both at the deciles of the base population, and reports the rejection rates of the rules PSI above 0.10, PSI above 0.25 and the chi-square benchmark over six pairs of sample sizes and 10,000 runs. The study of Demler, Pencina and D'Agostino compares two linear discriminants fitted on the
same sample, the larger with a fifth predictor that is unrelated to the outcome (8,261 observations, 621 cases, 1,000 repetitions), and finds a rejection rate of 0.001 for the DeLong test at the 5 percent level against an F-test close to 0.05.

The count tests have exact rejection probabilities, so that their size and power need no simulation. Each of the binomial, Vasicek-corrected and Jeffreys tests depends on the data only through the count $D$ and its p-value falls as $D$ grows; it rejects at level $\alpha$ exactly when $D\ge k^{*}$, the smallest count whose p-value is below $\alpha$ under the probability applied. Under a true probability $\pi$ and asset correlation $\rho$,
\begin{equation}
  P(\text{reject})=P_{\pi,\rho}(D\ge k^{*})=\int\bar F_{\mathrm{Bin}(N,\,p(x))}(k^{*}-1)\,\varphi(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad p(x)=\Phi\Bigl(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\pi)-\sqrt{\rho}\,x}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\Bigr),
  \label{eq:vt-exact}
\end{equation}
with $\bar F$ the survival function of the binomial law, and the binomial tail alone when $\rho=0$. The traffic-lights test with independent years has an exact distribution as well: the colour probabilities of each year, from its binomial count coloured by the test's own rule, are convolved over the years and summed over the profiles of the rejection region. \Cref{alg:vt-exact} states the first computation and \cref{alg:vt-rerun} the rerun of
one published cell.

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Exact rejection probability of a count test.}
\label{alg:vt-exact}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require registered test $\tau$, obligors $N$, probability applied $\mathrm{PD}$, level $\alpha$, true probability $\pi$ and true asset correlation $\rho$
\State $lo\gets0$, $hi\gets N$; \textbf{if} the p-value of $\tau$ at $D=N$ is not below $\alpha$ \textbf{return} 0 (no count rejects)
\While{$hi-lo>1$}
  \State $mid\gets\lfloor(lo+hi)/2\rfloor$; evaluate the registered test at $D=mid$
  \State \textbf{if} its p-value is below $\alpha$ \textbf{then} $hi\gets mid$ \textbf{else} $lo\gets mid$
\EndWhile
\State $k^{*}\gets hi$
\State \Return $\sum_{j=1}^{Q}w_j\,\bar F_{\mathrm{Bin}(N,p(x_j))}(k^{*}-1)$ with the $Q=256$ Gauss-Hermite nodes $x_j$ and weights $w_j$ of \cref{eq:vt-exact} (the binomial tail when $\rho=0$)
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[htbp]
\caption{Rerun of one cell of a published simulation study.}
\label{alg:vt-rerun}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require published rate $r'$ of $n'$ runs, scenario with its generator, test and rule, repetitions $n$, seed
\State spawn $n$ independent streams from the seed; for $i=1,\dots,n$ draw the data of the scenario from stream $i$
\For{$i=1,\dots,n$}
  \State apply the test to the data and read its p-value (or its metric for a rule on a metric); count an undefined result as a non-rejection and tally it separately
\EndFor
\State $k\gets$ number of rejections; $\hat r\gets k/n$; $\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}$ and the Wilson interval from \cref{eq:vt-mcse}
\State $\bar r\gets(k+r'n')/(n+n')$; $z\gets(\hat r-r')/\sqrt{\bar r(1-\bar r)(1/n+1/n')}$
\State \Return $(\hat r,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}},z,\ |z|\le3.29)$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\begingroup\emergencystretch=3em
\paragraph{Parameters, complexity and implementation.} The published studies fix the generators and the runs: \vtWpRuns{} runs for the working paper, \vtYnRuns{} for Yurdakul and Naranjo and \vtDmRuns{} for Demler and colleagues; the rerun of the working paper uses the same number of runs and compares each of the 144 printed rates of its Tables 7 and 8, 72 per test. The agreement bound 3.29 is the two-sided 0.1 percent
point, chosen so that the check is not triggered by Monte Carlo noise alone. The seed of the case is 42 and the repetitions of the size and power studies of case C22 are those of the tables of \cref{sec:results-validation-tests}. The cost of a rerun is $n$ times the cost of one evaluation of the test on one draw; the exact computation costs $O(Q\log N)$ for the count tests and $O(T\binom{T+3}{3})$ for the traffic-lights test over $T$ years. The implementation is
the module \vtfn{riskvalidation.harness} of \vtfn{riskvalidation} \vtEngineVersion{} (\vtfn{rates}: \vtfn{Rate}, \vtfn{wilson_interval}, \vtfn{size_bound}, \vtfn{within_size}, \vtfn{agrees}, \vtfn{agrees_with_published}; \vtfn{exact}: \vtfn{critical_count}, \vtfn{rejection_probability}, \vtfn{traffic_lights_rejection_probability}, \vtfn{wp14_true_confidence}; \vtfn{run}: \vtfn{simulate}),
the generators of \vtfn{riskvalidation.generators} (\vtfn{DefaultCounts}, \vtfn{TwoSample}, \vtfn{Migrations}, \vtfn{GradeFrequencies}, \vtfn{BinormalScores}) and the registry of named studies \vtfn{riskvalidation.generators.size_studies}, called by the pipeline modules \vtfn{c22_validator.py} and \vtfn{c22_studies.py} that write the documents of case C22.
\par\endgroup

The method compares each rerun with the printed value and against the exact probability where the test has one; the two references check one another, because an exact probability checks the generator, the harness and the test together. The rerun found three facts that the printed studies do not state. The traffic-lights cells of the working paper reproduce only with the tie rule that gives a boundary year the worse colour, not the better colour
of the printed mapping; with a whole number of expected defaults, which every scenario of the paper has, a year with exactly that many defaults sits on the boundary with probability between 5 and 37 percent, and the exact size of the test under the scenario with a probability of 3 percent over five years is \vtTlLowerExact{} percent with the printed rule and \vtTlUpperExact{} percent with the rule of the simulation, against 6.2 percent printed. The normal test is
above its nominal level at every level under independence and at the 0.5 and 0.1 percent levels in all eight scenarios of the working paper, although its summary calls it conservative. The Yurdakul and Naranjo rates of the rerun sit slightly above the printed ones, which the results report as a systematic offset.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results-validation-tests}

\paragraph{The published studies reproduce, with one cell of the working paper and four of Yurdakul and Naranjo outside the bound.} \Cref{tab:vt-published} and \cref{fig:vt-published} set the rerun against the printed rates. Of the \vtWpTotal{} cells of the working paper, \vtWpAgree{} agree within 3.29 pooled standard errors: all \vtWpNormalAgree{} cells of the normal test and \vtWpTrafficAgree{} of
\vtWpTrafficTotal{} of the traffic-lights test with the tie rule that gives the worse colour. The one cell outside the bound is listed in \cref{tab:vt-disagree}; the neighbouring levels of its row agree, and an independent run of 200,000 repetitions gives 0.9475 against the printed 0.955 (engine documentation), so the cell is stated as a disagreement and the printed value may be a misprint, which no source confirms.
Of the \vtYnTotal{} cells of Yurdakul and Naranjo, \vtYnAgree{} agree; the four outside the bound are in the same table, and they sit above the printed values. Over the \vtYnInner{} cells strictly between 0 and 1 the mean standardised difference is \vtYnMeanZ{}, where the three rules share the draws of each run, so that the cells come from \vtYnIndep{} independent runs (six pairs of sample sizes and three shifts) and a mean of 0 would carry a standard error of \vtYnSeOfMean{}. The offset has a cause the authors do not state, for example the treatment of an empty bin,
and the rerun did not identify it; every qualitative finding of the paper reproduces. The cell of Demler and colleagues reproduces: the DeLong test on nested models rejects \vtDmMeasured{} of the time at the 5 percent level against their \vtDmPublished{} in \vtDmRuns{} runs. What the figure does not show is the power of the rerun against a different seed; the number of agreeing cells of the Yurdakul and Naranjo study depends on the seed because the offset is of the order of the bound.

\paragraph{Most tests pass the size screen; the exceptions are known and follow from their definition.} \Cref{tab:vt-size} measures the size of the tests of the catalogue on data where the null holds at its boundary, from \vtNullReps{} repetitions. Of the \vtHoldSizeOf{} tests of the battery, \vtHoldSize{} pass the size screen at 5 and 1 percent, judged within the bound of \cref{eq:vt-sizebound} for a simulated rate and, where the test has an exact rejection probability, by that probability, which must not exceed the level. The two that do not are the normal test and the Jeffreys test, whose exact size at 1 percent is \vtJeffreysExactOne{} percent although its simulated rate, \vtJeffreysSimOne{} percent, is inside the bound. The Jeffreys test has an exact size of \vtJeffreysExact{}
percent at 5 percent for 1,000 obligors and a probability of 1 percent, the same as the binomial test (\vtBinomExact{}), because both reject from the same count; the Vasicek-corrected test, run at an assumed asset correlation of 12 percent on data generated at 12 percent, has an exact size of \vtVasicekExact{} percent. The normal test over five years rejects \vtNormalSize{} percent of right models at the 5 percent level, above its bound, as the working paper's own table prints under independence.
The traffic-lights test under the printed tie rule has an exact size of \vtTlLowerExact{} percent and a simulated one of \vtTlLowerSize{}; under the rule of the working paper's simulation it has \vtTlUpperExact{} and \vtTlUpperSize{}. The ECB concentration test and the migration z-tests are conservative: the migration test rejects \vtMigSize{} percent at its boundary, and the concentration test rejects none
(\cref{tab:vt-structure}). The estimator of the AUC variance checks the statistic the discrimination tests use: over the repetitions of the null the standard error of the ECB formula averages \vtAucModelSe{} against an exact value of \vtAucExactSe{}, the estimator has a bias of \vtAucBias{}, and the normal 95 percent interval covers \vtAucCover{} percent of the time. What the table does not show is a size at another sample size or probability.

\input{tables/validation-tests-size}

\Cref{tab:vt-settings} shows five choices of definition, four of which move the size and none of which a validator can read from the statistic's name. The Hosmer-Lemeshow statistic with $G-2$ degrees of freedom on a validation sample rejects \vtHlFittedSize{} percent of right models against \vtHlSize{} with $G$; the traffic-lights rule matters in the same way (\vtTlLowerSize{} percent against \vtTlUpperSize{}), whereas the thinnest grade of the chi-square test of the grades, with 0.6 expected defaults, leaves the size at \vtChiThin{} percent against \vtChiNull{}, a difference inside the Monte Carlo error, and
an AUC compared with a development AUC estimated on an equal sample rejects \vtAucInitDevOne{} percent of the time, which the extended variance brings back to \vtAucInitExt{} percent. The measured sizes are for these generators and sample sizes; a different sample or probability changes them.

\input{tables/validation-tests-settings}

\paragraph{Power against a miscalibrated probability, and the cost of the correlation correction.} \Cref{tab:vt-miscal} and \cref{fig:vt-power} give the power of the calibration tests when every grade's true probability exceeds the one applied by a factor $\kappa$. At $\kappa=1.25$ the Spiegelhalter test rejects \vtPowSpiegOneTwoFive{} percent of the time, the normal test \vtPowNormalOneTwoFive{}, the traffic-lights test \vtPowTlOneTwoFive{} (exact \vtPowTlOneTwoFiveExact{}), the Jeffreys test \vtPowJefOneTwoFive{}
and the binomial test \vtPowBinOneTwoFive{} (exact \vtPowBinOneTwoFiveExact{}), while the Hosmer-Lemeshow and chi-square tests, which spread the departure over groups, reject \vtPowHlOneTwoFive{} and \vtPowChiOneTwoFive{}. The Vasicek-corrected test, run at an assumed asset correlation of 12 percent on defaults that are independent, pays for its protection in power: it rejects \vtPowVasTwo{} percent at $\kappa=2$ and \vtPowVasThree{} percent at $\kappa=3$, because correcting for a correlation the defaults do not have costs power. The test of the default profile, which reads the shape and not the level, rejects \vtPowProfileOneFive{} percent
at $\kappa=1.5$, as it should when every grade is moved by the same factor. The exact probabilities agree with the simulated rates in all \vtExactCmpN{} comparisons of the table. The power is that of a planted factor at these sample sizes, not the probability of detecting a real bank's problem.

\label{fig:vt-power}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Correlated defaults overturn the independence-based tests; the corrected test holds its size only at the correlation it assumes.} \Cref{tab:vt-cluster} and \cref{fig:vt-clustering} set the correlation of the generator against the size of each test when the forecast probability is right. At an asset correlation of 5 percent the exact size of the binomial test at its 5 percent level is \vtClBinRhoFive{} percent and at 20 percent it is \vtClBinRhoTwoZero{}, in agreement with the simulation in all \vtClAgreeN{} of
\vtClAgreeOf{} comparisons. The Vasicek-corrected test, which assumes an asset correlation of 12 percent whatever the correlation that generated the data, has exact sizes of \vtClVasFive{}, \vtClVasOneZero{} and \vtClVasTwoZero{} percent when the true correlation is 5, 10 and 20 percent: it is conservative below the correlation it assumes and above its level at the highest, so it holds its size only where its assumed correlation is the true one. The chi-square test of the grades and the Hosmer-Lemeshow test reject
\vtClChiTwoZero{} and \vtClHlTwoZero{} percent at a correlation of 20 percent, the Spiegelhalter test \vtClSpTwoZero{}, and the normal test, which estimates the variance across years, moves from \vtClNormalZero{} percent at independence to \vtClNormalTwoZero{} at a correlation of 20 percent, with the traffic-lights test at \vtClTlTwoZero{}; the five-year panel of those two tests also carries a factor correlation of 0.2 between years whenever the asset correlation is positive, so that their numbers mix two changes. None of the tests that see one count, the grades or the obligors is robust to correlated defaults, which is the warning of the working paper restated with measured numbers; the normal test, whose variance estimate absorbs the correlation, falls to or below its level at correlations of 10 percent and above, and the traffic-lights test stays between \vtClTlTwoZero{} and \vtClTlMax{} percent.

\paragraph{Drift, discrimination decay and rating structure.} \Cref{tab:vt-drift} and \cref{fig:vt-drift} give the power against a mean shift of the scored variable and against a loss of AUC. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test is the most powerful against a shift of 0.1 standard deviations (\vtDrKsZeroOne{} percent against \vtDrPsiZeroOne{} for the benchmarked PSI), the PSI reaches \vtDrPsiZeroTwo{} percent at 0.2, and the calibration tests do not see a population shift at all: the Hosmer-Lemeshow and Spiegelhalter tests reject \vtDrHlZeroFive{}
and \vtDrSpZeroFive{} percent at a shift of 0.5, their size, because the model's probabilities stay right inside each bin. The ECB comparison with the development AUC is more powerful than DeLong against a loss of AUC (\vtDcAucZeroThree{} against \vtDcDelZeroThree{} percent at 0.03, \vtDcAucZeroFive{} against \vtDcDelZeroFive{} at 0.05), the two tests answer different questions, a fixed development AUC and a second model scored on the same obligors. DeLong rejects \vtLkNested{} percent on nested models and \vtLkNonNested{} percent on non-nested models of equal AUC, the
misuse of \citet{validation-tests:demler2012} reproduced. On the rating structure (\cref{tab:vt-structure}) the chi-square test on the counts sees a movement of 5 percent of every grade's mass into the modal grade \vtConChiFive{} percent of the time, against \vtConChiZero{} with no movement, while the ECB concentration test rejects at most \vtConHhiMax{} percent at any level of concentration, because its statistic is bounded below the critical value. The migration z-tests catch a cell twice its closer neighbour \vtBmRTwonFiveZeroZero{} percent of the time with 500 obligors per grade and \vtBmRTwonTwoZeroZeroZero{} with 2,000, and a cell 1.5 times its neighbour in \vtBmROneFivenFiveZeroZero{} and \vtBmROneFivenTwoZeroZeroZero{} percent of the samples.

\paragraph{The machine-learning and fairness tests pass the size screen and detect their planted defects.} \Cref{tab:vt-other} gives the four machine-learning and fairness tests that case C22 measures as named studies: the shift-resilience test has a size of \vtShiftSize{} percent and a power of \vtShiftPow{}, the conformal coverage test \vtConfSize{} and \vtConfPow{} percent, the two-proportion test \vtZSize{} and \vtZPow{}, and Fisher's exact test \vtFisherSize{} and \vtFisherPow{}. Across the \vtOtherStudies{} studies of the other families of the catalogue that case C22 also runs, the weakest power is \vtOtherPowMin{} percent,
the median \vtOtherPowMed{}, and \vtOtherAboveEightZero{} studies reach 80 percent. The wider planted-defect studies of the engine itself, with \vtMlConditions{} machine-learning conditions in \cref{tab:vt-ml-size} and \vtFairConditions{} fairness conditions in \cref{tab:vt-fair-size}, have a largest size of \vtMlSizeMax{} percent for the machine-learning tests, below the bound of \vtMlBoundTwoSe{} percent
that is the 5 percent level plus two Monte Carlo standard errors, and a smallest power of \vtMlPowerMin{} percent. Several nulls give a size of exactly zero and several defects a power of one, which shows only that the null and the defect of those studies are far apart; the study shows that the light can tell them apart, not where its boundary lies. The fairness tests have no size to speak of for the replication rule
when no effect exists, because the sign is then a coin flip, and the equal-opportunity test, which reads only the true positive rate, has a weak power against label noise (0.516 in the engine's table) while equalized odds detects it every time.

\paragraph{Case C20: the tests find an overfit model, an input-sensitive model and a planted leak.} \Cref{tab:vt-c20-lights} gives the lights of the machine-learning tests in the six variants of case C20, with \vtCtwentyRed{} red, \vtCtwentyAmber{} amber and \vtCtwentyGreen{} green rows, and \vtCtwentyNotEval{} not evaluated, over all of them, and \cref{tab:vt-c20-stats} the statistics behind them (\cref{fig:vt-c20}). The leakage screen catches the planted column: the single-feature AUC of the future-status code is
\vtCTwoZeroLeakAuc{}, the model's development AUC is \vtCTwoZeroDevAuc{} and its decision-time AUC \vtCTwoZeroDecAuc{}, and \vtCTwoZeroLeakViol{} feature values are dated after the observation date; the resemblance AUC of development against out-of-time is \vtCTwoZeroResAuc{}, so that this screen alone would have missed the leak, which is why the screens are read together. Input noise of 0.1 times each feature's spread costs the Taiwan
model \vtCTwoZeroRobLoss{} AUC points, a red light, against \vtCTwoZeroRobCtl{} points for the control run. Over 20 retraining seeds the AUC of the boosted model has a mean of \vtCTwoZeroSeedMean{} and a standard deviation of \vtCTwoZeroSeedSd{}, a green light, yet \vtCTwoZeroSeedFlip{} percent of the obligors change grade between seeds, the mean rank correlation of the attributions is \vtCTwoZeroSeedTau{} and the top-four reasons overlap only \vtCTwoZeroReasonLgbm{} and \vtCTwoZeroReasonXgb{} for the two models, an amber light:
a stable AUC does not make a stable explanation. The Shapley additivity gap of XGBoost is \vtCTwoZeroAddXgb{}, above the tolerance of $10^{-9}$ that the policy sets, while that of LightGBM is below it. On the Federal Reserve shift probes the observed drop in AUC on the worst subsample is \vtCTwoZeroSrDrop{} and its p-value against \vtCTwoZeroSrPerm{} development draws is \vtCTwoZeroSrP{}, the smallest value that $R=\vtCTwoZeroSrPerm{}$ draws can give, with a 95th percentile of the null drops of \vtCTwoZeroSrNullPNineFive{}; the conformal coverage of the 90 percent sets is \vtCTwoZeroCovBase{} in the baseline window, near the target, and \vtCTwoZeroCovPooled{} over the pooled windows, a red light. The findings are those of the planted
and public data; they say nothing of the quality of a bank's model.

\paragraph{Case C21: the same gap is found every year, with a stable size.} \Cref{tab:vt-c21-pairs} and \cref{tab:vt-c21-lights} give, for each of the \vtCTwoOnePairs{} year pairs on \vtCTwoOneRowsMin{} to \vtCTwoOneRowsMax{} rows per year, the disparity of Black against White applicants. The unconditional gap in approval rates is between \vtCTwoOneGapMin{} and \vtCTwoOneGapMax{} percentage points; after the permitted controls the odds ratio of approval lies between \vtCTwoOneOrMin{} and \vtCTwoOneOrMax{} with 95 percent intervals that never include 1
(\cref{fig:vt-c21}), and the coefficient refitted on the next year has between \vtCTwoOneRepMin{} and \vtCTwoOneRepMax{} of the size of the earlier one with the same sign. Over all pairs \vtCTwoOneZRed{} of \vtCTwoOneZN{} two-proportion tests are red, \vtCTwoOneAirAmber{} of \vtCTwoOneAirN{} four-fifths indicators are amber, and \vtCTwoOneRepAmber{} of \vtCTwoOneRepN{} replication rows change sign; the situation test finds between \vtCTwoOneStMin{} and \vtCTwoOneStMax{} percent
of the complainants significant, above the amber cut of 20 percent in \vtCTwoOneStAmber{} of the \vtCTwoOnePairs{} pairs. The controlled model lacks the credit score, which public mortgage data do not carry, so its estimate may be confounded by it; the statistics are indicators of comparative evidence and a finding of neither compliance nor violation, in the words of the interagency procedures, because gross approval-rate disparities cannot be attributed to a specific policy.

\paragraph{What follows for the use of the tests.} A validator who reads these tests together reads their sizes with them. The calibration tests built on independent defaults reject a right model several times as often as their level when defaults are correlated, so a red light of the binomial, Jeffreys, Hosmer-Lemeshow or chi-square test is evidence of miscalibration only after the correlation is stated; the Vasicek-corrected test is safe only at the correlation it assumes. The calibration tests do not see population drift, and the stability tests do not see miscalibration, so both
families are required. The ECB concentration test and the migration z-tests have little power in common settings, and the chi-square test on the counts is the substitute that the measurement supports. The machine-learning tests find the defects planted in them, and their lights are conventions that the engine labels so; the fairness tests find a stable disparity in the public mortgage decisions and state no legal claim.
